subject: chemistry
pattern: Carries about 7-8 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper: one 1-mark (IUPAC name, Swarts reaction or racemic mixture), one or two 2-mark reasoning or named-reaction questions, a 3-mark SN1/SN2 or haloarene reactivity question, and a 5-mark question on preparation or reactions. Examiners expect balanced equations with conditions, correct mechanism steps (transition state for SN2, carbocation for SN1) and the reason stated in one clear line.

questions.answer: A mixture containing equal amounts of the d- and l-enantiomers of a compound is called a racemic mixture. It is optically inactive because the rotation caused by one enantiomer is cancelled by the equal and opposite rotation of the other (external compensation). The process of conversion of an enantiomer into a racemic mixture is called racemisation.

questions.q: What is Swarts reaction? Give an example.
questions.answer: The reaction in which an alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg$_2$F$_2$, CoF$_2$ or SbF$_3$ to form an alkyl fluoride is called Swarts reaction. Example: CH$_3$Br + AgF → CH$_3$F + AgBr.

questions.q: Write the IUPAC name of (CH$_3$)$_3$C-CH$_2$-Br and of the compound C$_6$H$_5$-CH$_2$-Cl.
questions.answer: (CH$_3$)$_3$C-CH$_2$-Br: the longest chain has 3 carbons (propane) with two methyl groups and a bromine on the carbon numbered 1 and 2 respectively, so the name is 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane. C$_6$H$_5$CH$_2$Cl is named (chloromethyl)benzene (common name benzyl chloride).

questions.q: Haloalkanes are polar molecules but are insoluble in water. Give reason.
questions.answer: To dissolve a haloalkane in water, the new attractions between haloalkane and water molecules must be comparable to the strong hydrogen bonds already present between water molecules. Haloalkane-water attractions are weaker than water-water hydrogen bonds, so energy released is not enough to break the hydrogen bonds of water. Hence haloalkanes are only very slightly soluble in water, but dissolve readily in organic solvents.

questions.q: Distinguish between Sandmeyer reaction and Gattermann reaction.
questions.answer: Sandmeyer reaction: benzene diazonium chloride is treated with cuprous chloride or cuprous bromide dissolved in HCl or HBr to give chlorobenzene or bromobenzene. C$_6$H$_5$N$_2$Cl + CuCl/HCl → C$_6$H$_5$Cl + N$_2$. Gattermann reaction: the same conversion is done using freshly prepared copper powder with HCl or HBr instead of cuprous halide. C$_6$H$_5$N$_2$Cl + Cu/HCl → C$_6$H$_5$Cl + N$_2$ + CuCl. Yield in Gattermann reaction is generally lower.

questions.q: Why must Grignard reagents be prepared under anhydrous conditions? Write the reaction of Grignard reagent with water.
questions.answer: Grignard reagent RMgX contains a highly polar C-Mg bond in which carbon is strongly basic (carbanion character). It reacts with even traces of water (or any acidic hydrogen) and is destroyed, forming an alkane. RMgX + H$_2$O → R-H + Mg(OH)X. Hence dry ether and a moisture-free apparatus are used for its preparation.

questions.q: Write the equations for (i) Finkelstein reaction (ii) Wurtz reaction.
questions.answer: (i) Finkelstein reaction: an alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with NaI in dry acetone to give an alkyl iodide. R-Cl + NaI → R-I + NaCl (NaCl precipitates in acetone and drives the reaction forward). (ii) Wurtz reaction: alkyl halide is treated with sodium metal in dry ether to give a higher alkane with double the number of carbon atoms. 2R-X + 2Na → R-R + 2NaX.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide by SN1 mechanism.
questions.answer: SN1 is a two-step unimolecular reaction. Step 1 (slow, rate determining): the C-Br bond ionises to give a stable tertiary carbocation. (CH$_3$)$_3$C-Br → (CH$_3$)$_3$C$^+$ + Br$^-$. Step 2 (fast): the nucleophile OH$^-$ (or water) attacks the planar carbocation. (CH$_3$)$_3$C$^+$ + OH$^-$ → (CH$_3$)$_3$C-OH. Rate = k[(CH$_3$)$_3$CBr], first order in the haloalkane only. Tertiary halides react by SN1 because the carbocation is stabilised by three methyl groups through +I effect and hyperconjugation.

questions.q: Explain SN2 mechanism with the hydrolysis of bromomethane. What is the stereochemical outcome with an optically active halide?
questions.answer: SN2 is a one-step bimolecular reaction. The nucleophile OH$^-$ attacks the carbon from the side opposite to the leaving group Br (backside attack). A transition state is formed in which carbon is pentacoordinate, with partial bonds to both OH and Br. Then Br$^-$ leaves and CH$_3$OH is formed. Rate = k[CH$_3$Br][OH$^-$], second order. If the halide is optically active, the configuration is inverted (Walden inversion). Primary halides react fastest by SN2 because of less steric hindrance.

questions.q: Distinguish between SN1 and SN2 mechanisms (any three points).
questions.answer: SN1: (1) two-step reaction with carbocation intermediate; SN2: one-step reaction through a transition state. (2) SN1 rate depends on haloalkane only (first order); SN2 rate depends on both haloalkane and nucleophile (second order). (3) SN1 order of reactivity 3° > 2° > 1° > CH$_3$X; SN2 order is CH$_3$X > 1° > 2° > 3°. (4) SN1 gives racemisation of optically active halide; SN2 gives inversion of configuration. (5) SN1 is favoured by polar protic solvents; SN2 by polar aprotic solvents.

questions.q: Haloarenes are less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution than haloalkanes. Explain with three reasons.
questions.answer: (1) Resonance: the lone pair on halogen is delocalised into the benzene ring, giving the C-X bond partial double bond character, so it is harder to break. (2) Hybridisation: the carbon bearing halogen is sp$^2$ hybridised (more s-character, more electronegative) and holds the C-X bond more tightly than the sp$^3$ carbon of haloalkanes, so the bond is shorter and stronger. (3) Phenyl cation is not stabilised by resonance, so SN1 is not possible; the electron-rich benzene ring repels the approaching nucleophile, so SN2 is also not favoured.

questions.q: Mention any three harmful effects or uses of (i) chloroform (ii) DDT (iii) freons.
questions.answer: Chloroform: used as solvent and earlier as anaesthetic; on exposure to air and light it oxidises to poisonous phosgene (COCl$_2$), so it is stored in dark brown bottles filled to the brim; it damages liver. DDT: first synthetic insecticide used against malaria and lice; it is not metabolised and gets stored in fatty tissues, causing bioaccumulation and harm to birds and fish. Freons (CFCs): used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants; they reach the stratosphere and deplete the ozone layer.

questions.q: Explain with equations any five methods of preparation of haloalkanes.
questions.answer: (1) From alcohols with HX/ZnCl$_2$ (Lucas reagent): R-OH + HCl → R-Cl + H$_2$O. (2) From alcohols with PCl$_5$ or PCl$_3$: R-OH + PCl$_5$ → R-Cl + POCl$_3$ + HCl. (3) With thionyl chloride (best method, gaseous by-products): R-OH + SOCl$_2$ → R-Cl + SO$_2$ + HCl. (4) Free radical halogenation of alkanes (mixture of products): CH$_4$ + Cl$_2$ → CH$_3$Cl + HCl in UV light. (5) Addition of hydrogen halide to alkenes by Markovnikov rule: CH$_3$CH=CH$_2$ + HBr → CH$_3$CHBrCH$_3$. Also halogen exchange (Finkelstein, Swarts) gives iodides and fluorides.

questions.q: Explain the following reactions of haloalkanes with one example each: (i) nucleophilic substitution (ii) elimination (iii) reaction with magnesium (iv) Wurtz reaction.
questions.answer: (i) Nucleophilic substitution: halogen is replaced by a nucleophile. R-X + KOH(aq) → R-OH + KX; R-X + KCN → R-CN + KX; R-X + AgCN → R-NC. (ii) Elimination (dehydrohalogenation): heating with alcoholic KOH removes HX giving alkene; CH$_3$CH$_2$CHBrCH$_3$ + alc. KOH → but-2-ene (major, Saytzeff rule) + but-1-ene (minor). (iii) With Mg in dry ether, Grignard reagent forms: R-X + Mg → R-MgX. (iv) Wurtz reaction: 2CH$_3$Br + 2Na → CH$_3$CH$_3$ + 2NaBr in dry ether. Note: KCN gives alkyl cyanide (ionic, attacks through C) while AgCN gives isocyanide (covalent, attacks through N) - ambident nucleophile.

questions.q: Explain the following reactions of chlorobenzene with equations: (i) nitration (ii) halogenation (iii) Friedel-Crafts alkylation (iv) Wurtz-Fittig reaction. Why is halogen ortho-para directing though deactivating?
questions.answer: Electrophilic substitution gives mainly o- and p-isomers. (i) Nitration: conc. HNO$_3$ + conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ gives o- and p-nitrochlorobenzene (p major). (ii) Halogenation: Cl$_2$/anhydrous FeCl$_3$ gives o- and p-dichlorobenzene. (iii) Friedel-Crafts alkylation: CH$_3$Cl/anhyd. AlCl$_3$ gives o- and p-chlorotoluene. (iv) Wurtz-Fittig: C$_6$H$_5$Cl + CH$_3$Cl + 2Na in dry ether gives toluene (C$_6$H$_5$CH$_3$) + 2NaCl. Reason: by +R (resonance) effect the lone pair of halogen increases electron density at o- and p- positions, directing the electrophile there; but -I effect of the electronegative halogen withdraws electrons overall and deactivates the ring (reactions are slower than in benzene).
